title: Valuing Every Voice: The False Premise That 'Hands Up' Respondents Are More Worthy
author: Tom Sherrington
summary: This article challenges the pervasive classroom and organizational practice of relying on hand-raising to determine who speaks, arguing that this creates a contest for air time that systematically silences quieter students while falsely implying that volunteers are somehow more worthy of being heard. The author observes a strong gender bias in hand-raising cultures, with men and boys claiming disproportionate air time in both classrooms and staff meetings. The critical insight is that the practice of asking for volunteers assumes a merit in volunteering that does not exist: the person with their hand up does not know more, matter more, or deserve more attention than those who stay silent. Cold calling—directing questions to specific students rather than waiting for volunteers—is presented not as a clever pedagogical technique but as a solemn moral duty: ensuring that every voice is heard and given value. The article ends with a call for teachers and leaders to stop conducting discourse through volunteers and instead orchestrate it to invite, nurture, and bring in more marginal voices.
points: Hand-raising creates an involuntary contest for air time that systematically favors assertive personalities—disproportionately men and boys—while implying, falsely, that volunteers are more worthy of being heard than those who stay silent.

The child who sits quietly has ideas that are just as valid and interesting as those of the child with their hand up; the difference is not capability but willingness to enter the public contest for air time.

Cold calling is inclusive, invitational, and empowering—a signal that the teacher values every voice—but it is primarily a solemn moral duty, not merely a clever pedagogical strategy for attention management.

The same dynamic plays out in staff meetings, where dominant voices dominate repeatedly while quieter colleagues are never invited to share—creating a structural silence that no amount of good intention overcomes.

Teachers and leaders should orchestrate collective discourse rather than administering it through volunteers—making group conversation feel truly collective and ensuring that every voice, however quiet, is brought to the center.
quotes: just because somebody raises their hand does not mean they know more, matter more, deserve more air time, or are more worthy of being listened to.

The critical point is this: the adult or child who sits quietly, not feeling able or willing to enter the airtime contest, also has ideas. Crucially – so very obviously, but let’s spell it out – they matter just as much as anyone; their ideas are just as valid; their contributions are just as interesting and worthy of being explored as any of those with their hands up.

Cold calling, in this context, is the key. It’s inclusive, invitational, empowering. A signal of giving value to anyone and everyone. This, to me is a fundamental duty of any teacher – to ensure that every voice is heard; to give value to every voice.

Don't ask for volunteers. Don't let the dominant voices dominate again and again. Don't be that person – that teacher or leader. Be the one that orchestrates, that invites, that nurtures, that brings people in, that makes group discourse feel truly collective – where we listen to everyone however loud their voices are.

somebody usually puts their hand up because they invited into the contest: 'would anyone like to suggest…'; 'who can tell me…..'… 'does anyone want to share…..'? But.. BIG BIG BUT.. just because somebody raises their hand does not mean they know more.
It's not just some technical cogsci geekery; a cool pedagogical move to secure attention. It's a solemn duty; it's a matter of principle.
